title: Ang 1430: the last page
hook: the walk through the Granth is complete
tomorrow: why would anyone set an alarm for the dark before dawn?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seal: Guru Arjan's plate of truth, contentment and reflection, then a salok of thanks. The hymns are done. And yet there's a page after the seal.

Stay in your seat after a movie ends and the credits roll: the names of everyone who made the sound. The Guru Granth Sahib has something a little like that. After the seal comes the last page, and on it isn't another hymn. It's a list of ragas, the musical modes, set out in families, mode after mode. A holy book that closes with a music list. Why?
screen: `AFTER THE MOVIE: THE CREDITS.` → `AFTER THE SEAL: A LIST OF RAGAS.` → `WHY END ON MUSIC?`

segments.voice: The page is called the Raagmala, a garland of ragas. First, an honest part of the puzzle: Sikhs hold different views about it. Some read it aloud at the end of a full reading. Others close at the Mundavani and hold that the Raagmala isn't the Gurus' own bani. It sits in the printed Granth either way, and the question isn't settled among Sikhs. Now the solution, the part nobody disputes. Walk back through the whole book and see how it's built. After the opening prayers, the hymns are arranged by raga: Sri Rag, Majh, Gauri, Asa, on through the last raga, Jaijavanti. The Granth is a songbook. Its words were made to be sung, in kirtan, in a particular mood of music. So whatever you hold about the Raagmala, the last page points at the music the whole Guru lives in. And it is a whole Guru. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, passed the guruship to the Granth, and Sikhs bow to it as the living Guru, not a book about one. When a full reading ends, Sikhs often sing Anand Sahib, say Ardas, and share karah prashad. The walk is finished. Every page, from the first line to the last.
screen: `THE RAAGMALA: A GARLAND OF RAGAS.` · `SIKHS HOLD DIFFERENT VIEWS.` · `THE GRANTH IS A SONGBOOK.` · `THE GRANTH AS THE LIVING GURU.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE GURU.`

segments.voice: If you have a recording of Anand Sahib, play its opening and just listen. Its first line, in paraphrase: joy has come, mother, for I have found the True Guru. Let the music end, and let the sit hold the quiet after it.
Ang 1430. The last page: the Raagmala's list of ragas, read by some and closed before by others, and the end of the walk.
To keep: the whole guru, first page to last, every one walked. That's a long road, and it's done.

howItsDone: When a full reading of the Guru Granth Sahib ends, the congregation sings Anand Sahib, an Ardas is said, a hukam is taken and karah prashad is shared; congregations differ on whether the Raagmala is read before the close.

chat.says: WE FINISHED. bebe cried. then my cousin said the last page 'doesn't count'. is he right??
options: Sikhs differ on the Raagmala; some read it, some close at the seal. all bow to the whole Guru.
yes: the last page was printed by mistake, and every gurdwara skips it now.
no: the last page is the Guru's final command, so skipping it voids the reading.
chat.meaning: The Raagmala's place isn't settled among Sikhs: some read it, others end at the Mundavani. Either way, Sikhs bow to the Granth as the whole, living Guru.
